Instantiation is the act, process, or result of taking something general or abstract and turning it into (or representing it as) something specific and concrete.
The Most Important Concept: General vs. Specific

To understand instantiation, you first need to understand the relationship it describes — the relationship between a general thing (a type, a blueprint, a rule, an idea) and a specific thing (one real, particular example of that general thing).

That specific, concrete example is called an instance.

And instantiation is the act of creating or being that instance — the moment or process by which the specific example comes to exist, or the relationship that makes it an example of the general thing.

Think of it like this: if the general thing is a mold, then instantiation is the act of pouring metal into the mold to create one specific object. The object that comes out is the instance.

A recipe and a cake. A recipe is a general set of instructions. It describes, in the abstract, how a cake could be made. The actual cake you bake on Sunday afternoon is an instance of that recipe — it is one specific, real, physical cake that came from following those general instructions. The act of baking that specific cake is the instantiation of the recipe.

A law and a specific case. "No parking after 6 PM" is a general rule. When a specific car is ticketed on Tuesday at 7 PM on Oak Street, that ticketed event is an instantiation of the law — the general rule has been applied to, and has produced, a specific real-world case.

A word and its uses. The word "tree" exists as a general unit of language — an abstract entry in the dictionary, so to speak. Every single time someone says or writes "tree" in a sentence, that specific use is an instantiation of the word. Each use is one concrete occurrence of the general word.

A concept and a real thing. "Dog" is a general concept — it describes a type of creature. Your neighbor's specific dog, Bella, is an instantiation of that concept. She is one real, concrete, particular example of the general idea of "dog." She embodies it. She is it, made specific.

Philosophy has used this word for a long time, with great precision. Philosophers distinguish between:

Universals — abstract properties or concepts that can apply to many things (for example, "redness," "justice," or "roundness").

Particulars — specific, real, individual things that exist in the world (for example, this specific red apple sitting on your table).

When your red apple exists, it is said to be an instantiation of the property "redness." The apple is a particular, concrete thing that embodies the universal. Redness — as an abstract concept — is made real and specific in that apple.

In formal logic, instantiation means applying a general logical statement to a specific case. If the general rule is "All humans are mortal," then the specific statement "Socrates is mortal" is an instantiation of that rule — you have taken the general principle and applied it to one particular individual, producing a specific true statement about him.
In Computer Programming (its most common modern use)

This is where you'll hear the word most often today. In object-oriented programming (OOP), programmers write classes — these are essentially blueprints or templates that define what a certain type of thing should look like and how it should behave.

A class is general and abstract. It doesn't do anything on its own; it just describes a type of thing.

An object (also called an instance) is one specific, real thing that is created from that blueprint when the program runs.

Instantiation, in this context, is the act of creating a specific object from a class — the process of taking the general blueprint and producing one concrete, working thing from it.

Here is a concrete example to make this vivid: Imagine you write a class called Car. The class says, in the abstract, that every car has a color, a current speed, and can honk. The class itself is just a description — there is no actual car yet, just the idea of one. Now, when your program runs and creates a specific car — say, a red car currently going 60 mph — that is instantiation. You have taken the general blueprint (Car) and produced one specific, real object (a red car going 60 mph). That red car is an instance of the Car class. The act of creating it is instantiation.

You can instantiate a class as many times as you like, each time producing a different, independent instance — a blue car, a yellow car, a car going 0 mph. They all share the same blueprint (the class), but each is a separate, specific instance.

The word travels across many disciplines, always carrying the same core logic:

Linguistics draws a distinction between a word type (the word "tree" as an abstract unit of language) and a word token (each specific use of "tree" in a sentence). Every token is an instantiation of the type.

Mathematics uses it when you substitute specific values into a general formula or theorem. The general formula a² + b² = c² is abstract. When you plug in specific numbers — say, 3, 4, and 5 — you create an instantiation of that formula.

Cognitive science uses it to describe how a general mental concept becomes applied to a specific perceived thing — when your brain recognizes a specific face as "a human face," it has instantiated its general concept of "human face" onto that specific visual input.
Process vs. Result — A Subtle but Important Distinction

"Instantiation" can mean either:

The process — the act of creating the instance. "The instantiation of the object happened in the first line of the program." Here, instantiation refers to what happened — the creating.

The result — the specific instance that was created. "This red apple is an instantiation of the concept of redness." Here, instantiation refers to the thing itself — the apple as a realized example of the abstract property.

Both uses are correct. The word works for the act and for the outcome of the act.

Instantiation is the act, process, or result of a general, abstract, or blueprint-like thing being made concrete, specific, and real in a particular case. There is always a two-level relationship: something general (a class, a concept, a rule, a type, a blueprint) and something specific (an instance — a particular, real example of that general thing). Instantiation is what connects the two — it is the process of going from the general to the specific, or the relationship that makes the specific thing a real, concrete example of the general idea. You will find this word in philosophy, logic, computer programming, linguistics, mathematics, and beyond, but its meaning is always the same at heart: the general becomes real, specific, and concrete in one particular case.
